title: MATHMO: Automated Mathematical Modeling Through Adaptive Search
one_liner: A search method that automatically explores mathematical equations and frameworks to find models that balance speed, accuracy, and other real-world trade-offs, using an AI assistant to guide the exploration.
lead: Writing down equations to describe a real-world system — crop growth, river flow, particle motion — takes months of trial, error, and expert intuition. This paper asks: what if an AI system could automatically explore thousands of candidate equations and hand back the best ones? MATHMO does exactly that, treating the job as a systematic search problem with multiple conflicting goals (accurate predictions, simple equations, fast computation) and even subjective preferences.

paras: In fields like biology, engineering, and physics, building a mathematical model of reality means writing equations by hand. A researcher sits with data, hypothesizes a mechanism, proposes an equation, checks it against real measurements, tweaks the numbers, and repeats. This cycle takes months or years.

The core difficulty is that there are infinitely many equations you could try. Do you use a polynomial? Exponential growth? A differential equation with feedback loops? Each choice spawns sub-choices: how many terms, what order, which variables interact? A human expert navigates this space through intuition and luck.
A beginner would try all combinations exhaustively. This fails because the search space is huge, and many combinations are nonsensical or redundant.

callout.html: MATHMO automates the model-building search by having an AI assistant repeatedly propose candidate equations, score them on multiple objectives (speed, accuracy, simplicity), and iteratively refine the best ones.

steps.text: LLM proposes diverse mathematical frameworks (polynomial models, differential equations, etc.).
For each framework, generate multiple concrete equation variants.
Evaluate each model on data using speed, accuracy, and fit quality.
Find models that are not dominated — none is strictly better on all goals, because each represents a genuine trade-off worth keeping.
Zoom in on promising regions and tweak coefficient values and equation structure.

paras: A mathematical model is a choice of equation (or set of equations), the variables it uses, and the numbers multiplying each term (called coefficients). MATHMO's job is to explore this choice space and find models that work well. The paper does not change how you evaluate a model — you still test it against real data — but it systematically explores which models to test.

hidden.h2: The Pareto frontier: models that balance trade-offs
hidden.name: Pareto-efficient model set
paras: In the real world, you never have just one goal. You want a model that predicts accurately, runs fast, and stays simple enough to understand. These goals conflict: the most accurate model might be a huge neural network that runs slowly. The fastest model might be just a constant.

A Pareto-efficient set is the collection of models where no single model is better at every goal. If model A is faster than model B but less accurate, both are in the frontier because each excels in one dimension. MATHMO's goal is to discover this frontier — the set of models that represent genuine trade-offs, not obviously bad choices.

heat.caption: Highlighted models are on the Pareto frontier (no other model beats them on all criteria).

reads.html: The Pareto frontier is the set of model choices where you cannot improve one objective without hurting another, because they occupy different regions of the performance space — a fast model is slow-to-build, an accurate one is compute-heavy. MATHMO finds this set automatically by testing all candidates and filtering out obvious losers.
The paper uses Pareto optimization to balance multiple objectives (accuracy, computational cost, model simplicity, and subjective user preferences) without picking a single winner.

mechanism.h2: The search strategy: two levels of navigation
paras: Trying every equation combination is hopeless. MATHMO uses a two-level strategy. At the high level, an LLM explorer suggests diverse mathematical frameworks — should we use polynomial models, exponential growth, differential equations with feedback, or something else? At the low level, within each framework, the system refines the specific coefficients and equation structure.

Here is why this works: the LLM is good at high-level reasoning and exploring diverse ideas (that is what large language models do). The scoring function is good at checking whether an equation fits the data well. Together, they exploit the structure of the search space — frameworks cluster similar equations, so you do not jump around randomly.

stages.s: Real-world data and objectives (accuracy, speed, simplicity)
For each framework, generate candidate equations
Score candidates on all objectives using real data
Select models on the Pareto frontier
Set of models balancing speed, accuracy, simplicity

math.h2: Balancing multiple objectives with a score function
math.words: For each model, compute a weighted sum of scores: overall_score = w_accuracy * accuracy_score + w_speed * speed_score + w_simplicity * simplicity_score, where w_accuracy, w_speed, w_simplicity are weights chosen by the user to reflect how much each goal matters.
math.equation: score_total = w_acc * (1 - error_rate) + w_speed * (1 / compute_time) + w_simple * (1 / num_terms)
symbols: how far predictions deviate from real data (0 = perfect, 1 = useless)
how long the model takes to predict one output (in milliseconds)
the number of terms in the equation (more terms = harder to interpret)
weight for accuracy importance (user sets this)
weight for speed importance (user sets this)
weight for simplicity importance (user sets this)
the combined score a model gets on all three objectives

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Model A: error_rate = 0.1, compute_time = 5ms, num_terms = 3 terms. Weights: w_acc = 0.5, w_speed = 0.3, w_simple = 0.2.
Model B: error_rate = 0.05, compute_time = 20ms, num_terms = 8 terms. Accuracy: 0.5 * 0.95 = 0.475. Speed: 0.3 * 0.05 = 0.015. Simplicity: 0.2 * 0.125 = 0.025. Total: 0.515.
Model A scores higher (0.577 vs 0.515) because our weights favor accuracy and simplicity; Model B is more accurate but slower and more complex.

math.note: The equation translates user preferences into a score that ranks candidate models fairly on all dimensions, allowing the search to find trade-offs rather than false winners.

bars.h2: Comparing manual modeling to automated search

charts.title: Manual expert search
charts.note: An expert might try 10–20 model ideas over months, guided by intuition. Most time is spent on dead ends.

charts.title: MATHMO automated search
charts.note: MATHMO tests hundreds of models in hours, because the LLM guides exploration and scoring is fast. It finds genuine trade-off frontiers, not just one winner.

items.html: If the LLM does not understand the domain, it may suggest equations that are mathematically invalid or nonsensical for the application. Example: proposing a polynomial model for a system that is fundamentally exponential. Mitigation: seed the LLM with domain context and examples.

If you do not include an objective in the score function (e.g., numerical stability, interpretability for regulators), MATHMO will optimize for what you told it to and ignore the rest. The frontier will be misleading.

A complex equation might fit the historical data perfectly but fail on new data. MATHMO's score can be misled if it evaluates models only on one data snapshot. Mitigation: use cross-validation or held-out test data to score candidates.

Include domain knowledge in the LLM prompt, score on all real objectives (and separate training from test data), and iteratively refine the preference weights as you learn what trade-offs actually matter.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should pick a real-world dataset with multiple, conflicting objectives. Example: modeling the spread of a disease in a population. You want accuracy (predictions match real case counts), but also speed (the model must run on a mobile device), and simplicity (health officials must understand the mechanism). Run MATHMO to search for models, plot the Pareto frontier, and show that each model on the frontier represents a real trade-off — improving one goal breaks another.
demo.metric_eq: frontier_coverage = (number of Pareto-optimal models found) / (true size of frontier), computed by comparing MATHMO's results to models humans generated in the same time budget.
demo.closing: The demo must show that MATHMO discovers models a human would have taken weeks to find, and that the frontier genuinely represents trade-offs (not just a list of bad models).
